title: FMCSA / US DOT Jurisdiction over Motor Carriers — Overview
agency: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) / U.S. DOT
applies_to: Any employer that operates a commercial motor vehicle (CMV) in interstate commerce — GVWR/GVW of 10,001 lbs or more, vehicles designed to carry 9+ passengers for compensation (or 16+ not for compensation), or any size vehicle hauling placardable hazardous materials. This is a SEPARATE regulatory system from OSHA: FMCSA governs highway/commercial-vehicle safety, OSHA governs the worksite. A field-service contractor with pickups and trailers over 10,001 lbs is very often a regulated motor carrier without realizing it.
summary: FMCSA administers the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSRs), 49 CFR Parts 350-399, plus the DOT-wide drug & alcohol testing procedures in Part 40. The compliance a carrier is graded on clusters into a handful of buckets that also drive prequalification grades (ISN, Avetta, Veriforce): (1) operating authority & registration — the USDOT number and the biennial MCS-150 update (Part 390); (2) the CSA Safety Measurement System and its seven BASICs, fed by roadside inspections and crashes; (3) driver qualification files (Part 391); (4) the controlled-substances & alcohol program and the Clearinghouse (Parts 382 & 40); (5) hours of service and ELDs (Part 395); (6) vehicle inspection, repair, maintenance and the DVIR (Part 396); (7) CDL/ELDT (Parts 383/380); (8) financial responsibility/insurance (Part 387); and (9) the safety rating from a compliance review (Part 385). A public hit in any of these — a low CSA BASIC, a Conditional/Unsatisfactory safety rating, a deactivated USDOT number — instantly damages a prequal grade and is the classic warm reverse-lead trigger.
key_requirements: Obtain and maintain an active USDOT number (and MC operating authority if for-hire).
Keep the MCS-150 updated at least every 24 months (Part 390.19) — lapse deactivates the USDOT number.
Maintain a compliant driver qualification file for every driver (Part 391).
Run a DOT drug & alcohol testing program and query/report to the Clearinghouse (Parts 382 & 40).
Comply with hours-of-service limits and run compliant ELDs (Part 395).
Run a systematic inspection/repair/maintenance program with DVIRs and annual inspections (Part 396).
Carry the minimum financial responsibility for the cargo/service (Part 387).
deadlines: MCS-150 biennial update on the schedule set by the USDOT number's last two digits
New Entrant Safety Audit within the first 12 months of operation
penalty_structure: Civil penalties under 49 U.S.C. 521(b) and 14901, adjusted annually for inflation; ranges from a few thousand dollars per record-keeping violation up to five and six figures for out-of-service and hazmat violations, plus out-of-service orders and USDOT deactivation.
failure_points: Assuming 'we're not a trucking company' when pickups/trailers exceed 10,001 lbs GVWR.
Letting the USDOT number go inactive by missing the biennial MCS-150.
No written DOT drug & alcohol policy or no Clearinghouse queries.
Thin driver qualification files (missing MVRs, medical cards, prior-employer inquiries).
source: 49 CFR Chapter III (FMCSA); DOT Part 40; FMCSA.gov / eCFR
notes: Origin supports the DOCUMENTATION and program side — it is not legal counsel and does not file for the carrier. Reference layer only.

title: Part 390 — USDOT Registration & the Biennial MCS-150 Update (390.19)
agency: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) / U.S. DOT
applies_to: Every motor carrier, intermodal equipment provider, and hazmat shipper required to have a USDOT number. This is the single most common FMCSA lead trigger because a deactivated USDOT number is public and instantly fails prequal.
summary: A carrier must file Form MCS-150 (Motor Carrier Identification Report) to obtain a USDOT number and must UPDATE it at least once every 24 months, even if nothing changed and even if the carrier has stopped operating (in which case it files to deactivate). The update month is fixed by the USDOT number: the next-to-last digit tells whether the update is due in an even or odd year, and the last digit maps to the month. 49 CFR 390.19(b)(4) is the specific paragraph requiring the biennial update; failing it lets FMCSA (a) assess a civil penalty under 49 U.S.C. 521(b)(2)(B) or 14901(a), and (b) DEACTIVATE the USDOT number. A deactivated number means the carrier shows as not registered — which reads as an automatic fail on ISN/Avetta/Veriforce and to any hiring client checking SAFER. The fix is straightforward: refile/verify the MCS-150 (or MCSA-1 under URS), correct fleet size, mileage, driver count, and operation classification, and confirm reactivation on SAFER. Part 390.21 separately requires the USDOT number (and, for for-hire, the legal name) be marked legibly on both sides of each self-propelled CMV.
key_requirements: File MCS-150 to obtain the USDOT number before operating in interstate commerce.
Update the MCS-150 at least every 24 months per the number-based schedule (390.19(b)).
Update within the required window after any change to the information (name, address, fleet, operation).
File to deactivate if the carrier ceases interstate operations.
Display the USDOT number (and legal/DBA name) on both sides of each CMV (390.21).
deadlines: Biennial update month = fixed by the last two digits of the USDOT number (next-to-last digit: even year vs odd year; last digit: month 1-0 = Jan-Oct... per FMCSA's published table).
penalty_structure: Civil penalty up to the inflation-adjusted maximum per day of violation (statutory basis 49 U.S.C. 521(b)(2)(B); commonly cited around $1,000+/day to a capped maximum), PLUS deactivation of the USDOT number until the update is filed.
failure_points: Believing the update is only needed 'when something changes' — it is required every 24 months regardless.
Never getting FMCSA's reminder because the address on file is stale.
Discovering the deactivation only when a hiring client's prequal check fails.
Refiling with wrong fleet/mileage numbers, which can shift the carrier's CSA exposure.
notes: This is the code Origin's Lead Radar surfaces most. Helping here = verify the MCS-150, refile it correctly, confirm reactivation. Documentation support only, not a legal filing service.

title: CSA & the Safety Measurement System — the 7 BASICs
citation: FMCSA CSA program; SMS Methodology (Part 385 context)
agency: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) / U.S. DOT
applies_to: Every carrier with a USDOT number that accrues roadside inspections or crashes. CSA percentiles are the single biggest driver of a prequal safety grade.
summary: Compliance, Safety, Accountability (CSA) is FMCSA's enforcement model. Its Safety Measurement System (SMS) rolls up 24 months of roadside inspection violations and crashes into seven Behavior Analysis and Safety Improvement Categories (BASICs): (1) Unsafe Driving, (2) Crash Indicator, (3) Hours-of-Service Compliance, (4) Vehicle Maintenance, (5) Controlled Substances/Alcohol, (6) Hazardous Materials Compliance, and (7) Driver Fitness. Each violation is weighted by severity and time; carriers are ranked into a 0-100 percentile against peers with similar inspection volume — HIGHER is WORSE. When a BASIC crosses its intervention threshold (roughly 65% for most, 60% for passenger/hazmat carriers, and 50%/55% for Unsafe Driving and HOS), the carrier is prioritized for FMCSA intervention and the number becomes a red flag on prequal. Only some BASIC data is public (Unsafe Driving, HOS, Vehicle Maintenance, Hazmat, Driver Fitness are shown as alerts; Crash Indicator and Controlled Substances are not publicly displayed). The way to move a score is to (a) reduce new violations, (b) let old ones age out of the 24-month window, and (c) remove violations that are wrong or misattributed via DataQs.
key_requirements: Monitor the SMS profile monthly for BASIC percentiles and alerts.
Target the worst-performing BASIC first (it's usually driving the prequal grade).
Coach drivers on the specific violation types that are scoring against the carrier.
Challenge incorrect or non-preventable events through DataQs.
forms: FMCSA SMS carrier profile (login via FMCSA Portal)
deadlines: Violations weight down and age out over a rolling 24 months.
penalty_structure: CSA scores are not themselves fines, but crossing thresholds triggers FMCSA interventions (warning letters, investigations, compliance reviews) that can lead to penalties and a downgraded safety rating.
failure_points: Ignoring the SMS until a hiring client flags it.
Chasing every BASIC instead of the one dragging the grade.
Leaving wrong violations on the record instead of filing DataQs.
source: FMCSA CSA / SMS Methodology; FMCSA Portal
notes: Reading and explaining a carrier's BASICs is exactly the kind of plain-English translation Origin can do. Reference only.

title: DataQs — Challenging Wrong Inspection & Crash Records
citation: FMCSA DataQs system (Request for Data Review)
agency: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) / U.S. DOT
applies_to: Any carrier or driver who believes a roadside inspection violation, crash, or other record in FMCSA data is incorrect, misassigned, or non-preventable.
summary: DataQs is FMCSA's online portal for filing a Request for Data Review (RDR) to correct information in federal safety systems — the very data that feeds CSA/SMS and the carrier's prequal grade. Common, high-value challenges: a violation assigned to the wrong carrier, a duplicate inspection, a citation dismissed or reduced in court (an adjudicated result can change the DataQs outcome), a crash that was clearly not the driver's fault (the Crash Preventability Determination Program covers defined non-preventable crash types), or an inspection with a clerical error (wrong VIN, wrong USDOT). The RDR is routed to the state agency or FMCSA division that submitted the record, which reviews and either upholds or removes it. Because CSA is built from this data, removing even a few wrongly-attributed severe violations can drop a BASIC below its intervention threshold — one of the fastest, lowest-cost ways to improve a score. Good DataQs practice: attach the supporting evidence (court disposition, photos, the inspection report, dashcam), be specific about the CFR paragraph, and track the response.
key_requirements: Pull the carrier's inspection and crash history from the SMS profile.
Identify records that are wrong, duplicated, adjudicated away, or non-preventable.
File a Request for Data Review with specific evidence.
Use the Crash Preventability Determination Program for eligible non-preventable crash types.
deadlines: No universal deadline, but crash-preventability requests have program-specific eligibility windows; file promptly while evidence is fresh.
penalty_structure: None — DataQs is a correction mechanism, not an enforcement action.
failure_points: Filing without evidence (RDRs get denied).
Not challenging court-dismissed citations (they can still be scoring in CSA).
Missing the crash-preventability program for eligible crash types.
source: FMCSA DataQs; Crash Preventability Determination Program
notes: One of the strongest 'free look' offers for a carrier lead: review the inspection history and spot the challengeable records. Documentation support only.

title: Part 391 — Driver Qualification (DQ) Files
agency: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) / U.S. DOT
applies_to: Every motor carrier, for each driver who operates a CMV. DQ files are the most-cited paperwork gap in compliance reviews and prequal audits.
summary: Part 391 sets who is qualified to drive and what the carrier must keep on file to prove it. 49 CFR 391.51 lists the required contents of the driver qualification file: the employment application (391.21); the results of the safety-performance-history investigation and inquiries to prior DOT-regulated employers (391.23), which is where the Pre-Employment Screening Program (PSP) report fits; the motor vehicle record (MVR) obtained at hire and the annual review of driving record (391.25); the driver's certificate/list of violations (391.27); the road test certificate or an accepted equivalent (391.31/391.33); and the medical examiner's certificate plus National Registry verification (391.41/391.43/391.45), along with a Skill Performance Evaluation certificate or entry-level driver training certificate where applicable. Files must be kept for the duration of employment plus three years. Thin or missing DQ files are a top finding in FMCSA compliance reviews (Driver Fitness BASIC) and a routine ISN/Avetta document request.
key_requirements: Employment application meeting 391.21 (3-year employment history, accident/violation history).
Prior-employer safety performance history inquiries within 30 days of hire (391.23).
MVR at hire and an annual review of the driving record (391.25).
Annual driver's certificate/list of violations (391.27).
Road test certificate or equivalent (391.31/391.33).
Current medical examiner's certificate from a National Registry examiner (391.43/391.45).
deadlines: Prior-employer inquiries within 30 days of hire
Annual MVR review
Annual certificate of violations
Medical certificate renewed per its expiration (max 24 months, often shorter)
penalty_structure: Per-violation civil penalties for missing DQ-file elements; contributes to the Driver Fitness BASIC and can support a Conditional/Unsatisfactory rating.
failure_points: Missing prior-employer safety-history inquiries (391.23).
Expired medical certificates still in the file.
No annual MVR review or no certificate of violations.
No road test certificate or acceptable equivalent.
notes: Building and auditing DQ-file packages is core documentation work for Origin. Reference only.

title: Parts 382 & 40 — DOT Controlled Substances & Alcohol Program
agency: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) / U.S. DOT
applies_to: Every employer of CDL drivers operating CMVs in commerce. Part 40 governs HOW the tests are done DOT-wide; Part 382 governs WHO/WHEN for motor carriers.
summary: A carrier that employs CDL drivers must run a compliant DOT drug & alcohol testing program with six test types: pre-employment (drug test with a verified negative before performing safety-sensitive functions), random (annual minimum rates set by FMCSA — commonly 50% for controlled substances and 10% for alcohol, subject to annual adjustment), post-accident (per the 382.303 criteria), reasonable suspicion (based on trained-supervisor observation), return-to-duty, and follow-up (directed by a Substance Abuse Professional). Part 40 dictates the collection, chain of custody, laboratory, Medical Review Officer (MRO) verification, and SAP return-to-duty process. The carrier needs a written policy distributed to drivers, supervisor reasonable-suspicion training, a designated employer representative, an MRO and consortium/TPA relationship, and records retained per 382.401. Program gaps are cited under the Controlled Substances/Alcohol BASIC and are a standard prequal document request.
key_requirements: Written DOT drug & alcohol policy provided to every driver.
Pre-employment drug test with verified negative before safety-sensitive duty.
Random testing at or above FMCSA's annual minimum rates.
Post-accident, reasonable-suspicion, return-to-duty, and follow-up testing.
Supervisor reasonable-suspicion training; designated employer representative; MRO.
Records retained per 382.401 with confidentiality controls.
deadlines: Pre-employment before first safety-sensitive function
Random spread across the calendar year
MIS data on request; retention periods per 382.401
penalty_structure: Per-violation civil penalties; a driver who tests positive or refuses must be immediately removed from safety-sensitive duty; program failures feed the Controlled Substances/Alcohol BASIC.
failure_points: No written policy or outdated policy citing wrong rates.
Not enrolled in a random-testing consortium / not meeting the minimum rate.
No supervisor reasonable-suspicion training.
Letting a driver work before the verified pre-employment negative.
notes: Origin builds the written program and the recordkeeping framework; it does not act as MRO/SAP/collector. Reference only.

title: Drug & Alcohol Clearinghouse (Part 382 Subpart G)
agency: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) / U.S. DOT
applies_to: Every employer of CDL/CLP drivers and their consortia/TPAs, MROs, and SAPs.
summary: The FMCSA Commercial Driver's License Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse is the federal database of CDL drivers' drug and alcohol program violations. Employers must register, obtain each driver's consent, and run queries: a full pre-employment query before hire, and at least one query per year (limited or full, with consent) for every current CDL driver. Employers, MROs, and SAPs must also REPORT violations, refusals, negative return-to-duty results, and completion of follow-up testing to the Clearinghouse. Since November 2024 ('Clearinghouse-II'), state driver licensing agencies must act on Clearinghouse 'prohibited' status — a driver in prohibited status can have the CDL downgraded, so keeping queries and RTD documentation current is now tied directly to license validity. Missing annual queries is a frequent, easily-cited gap and a standard prequal document request.
key_requirements: Register in the Clearinghouse and designate access.
Full pre-employment query (with driver's electronic consent) before hire.
At least one query per year for every current CDL driver.
Report violations, refusals, RTD, and follow-up completion as required.
Retain query results and consents (3 years).
deadlines: Pre-employment query before hire
At least annually thereafter for each driver
Report violations promptly per 382.705
penalty_structure: Civil penalties for failing to query or report; a driver in prohibited status may not perform safety-sensitive functions and faces CDL downgrade by the state.
failure_points: Skipping the annual limited query for existing drivers.
No documented driver consent on file.
Not reporting a violation the employer is required to report.
notes: Documentation/tracking support only — Origin does not run queries on the carrier's behalf. Reference only.

title: Part 395 — Hours of Service & Electronic Logging Devices
agency: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) / U.S. DOT
applies_to: Drivers of property- and passenger-carrying CMVs and the carriers that employ them.
summary: Part 395 caps how long a driver may work and drive and requires most drivers to log duty status electronically. For property-carrying drivers the core limits are: 11 hours maximum driving after 10 consecutive hours off duty; a 14-hour on-duty window that driving may not extend beyond; a required 30-minute break after 8 cumulative hours of driving; and a 60-hours/7-days or 70-hours/8-days limit that can reset with 34 consecutive hours off ('34-hour restart'). Short-haul and adverse-conditions exceptions apply. The ELD mandate requires a registered, compliant electronic logging device to record duty status automatically (with narrow grandfather and short-haul exemptions); carriers have responsibilities to manage unassigned driving time and edits (395.22), drivers have responsibilities to certify and annotate (395.24), and both must handle ELD malfunctions and data-diagnostic events (395.34). HOS/ELD violations feed the HOS Compliance BASIC and are among the most common roadside out-of-service items.
key_requirements: Enforce the 11-hour driving / 14-hour window / 30-minute break limits.
Enforce the 60/70-hour limits and document any 34-hour restart.
Use a registered, compliant ELD unless a valid exemption applies.
Manage unassigned driving time, edits, and driver certifications (395.22/395.24).
Have an ELD malfunction/data-diagnostic procedure and 8-day paper-log backup (395.34).
forms: Driver's record of duty status (ELD or approved paper log)
deadlines: Daily duty-status certification; supporting documents retained 6 months; ELD backups per 395.34
penalty_structure: Per-violation civil penalties; serious HOS violations trigger driver/vehicle out-of-service orders and score heavily in the HOS BASIC.
failure_points: Unassigned driving time not resolved.
Form-and-manner errors on logs / missing supporting documents.
Using a non-registered ELD or claiming a short-haul exemption that doesn't apply.
notes: Origin supports the written HOS/ELD policy and recordkeeping practice, not the telematics itself. Reference only.

title: Part 396 — Inspection, Repair, Maintenance & the DVIR
agency: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) / U.S. DOT
applies_to: Every motor carrier and intermodal equipment provider, for every CMV operated.
summary: Part 396 requires a systematic program to inspect, repair, and maintain every CMV, with records that prove it. 396.3 requires the systematic maintenance program plus maintenance records (identification of the vehicle, nature and due dates of inspections/maintenance, and repair records) kept for the required period. 396.11 requires the Driver Vehicle Inspection Report (DVIR): a driver must report defects that affect safety at the end of each driving day, the carrier must certify repairs (or that none were needed), and the next driver must review. 396.13 requires the driver's pre-trip review. 396.17 requires a periodic (annual) inspection meeting Appendix A standards, documented and kept, with the inspector meeting the qualification standards of 396.19; brake inspectors must meet 396.25. Vehicle Maintenance is a public CSA BASIC, and maintenance/DVIR paperwork is a routine prequal and compliance-review request.
key_requirements: Written systematic inspection/repair/maintenance program (396.3).
Maintenance records per vehicle retained for the required period.
Daily DVIR with defect reporting, carrier repair certification, next-driver review (396.11).
Pre-trip inspection by the driver (396.13).
Annual periodic inspection to Appendix A, by a qualified inspector (396.17/396.19).
Qualified brake inspectors (396.25).
deadlines: DVIR each driving day when defects exist
Periodic inspection at least every 12 months
Maintenance records retained per 396.3 (generally 12 months, longer after the vehicle leaves the fleet)
penalty_structure: Per-violation civil penalties; safety-critical defects result in out-of-service orders; scores in the Vehicle Maintenance BASIC.
failure_points: No annual inspection on file or unqualified inspector.
DVIRs with no carrier repair certification.
No documented systematic maintenance program — just ad-hoc repairs.
source: 49 CFR Part 396 incl. Appendix A; FMCSA
notes: Origin builds the maintenance program and DVIR recordkeeping framework. Reference only.

title: Part 393 — Parts & Accessories and Cargo Securement
agency: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) / U.S. DOT
applies_to: Every CMV operated by a motor carrier; the cargo-securement rules apply to how loads are restrained.
summary: Part 393 sets the minimum equipment a CMV must have and keep in working order — brakes, lamps and reflectors, glazing, coupling devices, emergency equipment, frames, tires, and steering — and, in Subpart I (393.100-393.136), the North American cargo securement standard. The securement rules set minimum performance criteria (a load must be restrained against a defined fraction of its weight in forward, rearward, and lateral forces), an aggregate working-load-limit rule (total securement WLL at least 50% of cargo weight), tiedown counts based on article length and weight, and commodity-specific rules (logs, metal coils, vehicles, heavy machinery, etc.). Loose or missing securement and equipment defects are common roadside out-of-service violations and feed the Vehicle Maintenance BASIC.
key_requirements: Keep all required parts/accessories in safe working order (lamps, brakes, tires, coupling, emergency equipment).
Secure cargo to the Subpart I performance criteria (restraint against forward/rear/lateral forces).
Meet aggregate working-load-limit (>=50% of cargo weight) and tiedown-count rules.
Apply the commodity-specific rules for the load being hauled.
forms: Load securement / tiedown records where used
deadlines: Continuous — checked pre-trip and at roadside; re-check securement during trip per 392.9.
penalty_structure: Per-violation civil penalties; unsecured loads and equipment defects trigger out-of-service and score in Vehicle Maintenance.
failure_points: Insufficient tiedowns for the article's length/weight.
Damaged or under-rated securement devices.
Missing emergency equipment or inoperative lamps.
source: 49 CFR Part 393 incl. Subpart I; FMCSA

title: Parts 383 & 380 — CDL Standards and Entry-Level Driver Training
agency: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) / U.S. DOT
applies_to: Drivers required to hold a CDL and the carriers who employ them; training providers on the FMCSA Training Provider Registry.
summary: Part 383 sets who must hold a Commercial Driver's License, the single-license rule, vehicle groups (A/B/C), endorsements (H hazmat, N tank, P passenger, S school bus, T doubles/triples) and restrictions, the disqualifying offenses (383.51), and the knowledge/skills standards. Part 380 Subpart F is the Entry-Level Driver Training (ELDT) rule: since February 7, 2022, anyone obtaining a first CDL, upgrading a class, or getting a first H/P/S endorsement must complete theory and behind-the-wheel training from a provider listed on FMCSA's Training Provider Registry before taking the skills (or, for hazmat, knowledge) test. Carriers verifying a new CDL hire should confirm the correct class/endorsements, no disqualifications, and, for new entrants to the industry, that ELDT was completed and recorded in the Registry.
key_requirements: Verify the driver holds the correct CDL class and endorsements for the vehicle/cargo.
Confirm no disqualifying offenses under 383.51.
For first-time/upgrading CDL holders, confirm ELDT completion via the Training Provider Registry.
Maintain single-license compliance (one CDL only).
deadlines: ELDT before the skills/knowledge test for covered applicants (on/after 2/7/2022).
penalty_structure: Per-violation civil penalties; disqualifications remove the driver from CMV operation; feeds Driver Fitness.
failure_points: Hiring a driver whose endorsements don't match the cargo (e.g., no H for placarded hazmat).
Missing ELDT verification for a first-time CDL holder.
source: 49 CFR Parts 383 & 380; FMCSA Training Provider Registry

title: Part 387 — Minimum Financial Responsibility (Insurance)
agency: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) / U.S. DOT
applies_to: For-hire and certain private motor carriers of property and passengers in interstate commerce.
summary: Part 387 sets the minimum public-liability (bodily injury, property damage, environmental restoration) insurance a carrier must carry, evidenced by endorsements filed with FMCSA. For general freight the baseline is $750,000; for non-hazardous property in vehicles under 10,001 lbs it can be lower, while hazmat can require $1,000,000 or $5,000,000 depending on the commodity. Passenger carriers require $1,500,000 (16 or fewer seats) or $5,000,000 (more than 16). Proof is filed on Form BMC-91/BMC-91X (or a trust/surety alternative), and the MCS-90 endorsement attaches to the policy to guarantee statutory minimums to the public. Prequal platforms and hiring clients routinely require a Certificate of Insurance meeting or exceeding these limits plus contractual additional-insured/waiver language.
key_requirements: Carry at least the applicable minimum public-liability limit for the cargo/service.
File the required proof (BMC-91/BMC-91X) and carry the MCS-90 endorsement where applicable.
Provide Certificates of Insurance meeting hiring-client/prequal limits.
deadlines: Continuous coverage; filings updated on change of insurer.
penalty_structure: Operating without required coverage can revoke operating authority and carries civil penalties.
failure_points: Coverage below the hiring client's contractual limit (fails prequal even if it meets the federal floor).
No MCS-90 where required; expired COI on the prequal platform.
notes: Origin does not place insurance; it helps assemble/track the required proofs and COIs. Reference only.

title: Part 385 — Safety Ratings, Compliance Reviews & the New Entrant Audit
citation: 49 CFR Part 385 (incl. Subpart A ratings, Subpart D New Entrant)
agency: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) / U.S. DOT
applies_to: Every motor carrier subject to FMCSA, especially new entrants in their first 12 months and any carrier selected for investigation.
summary: Part 385 is how FMCSA assigns a carrier's safety rating — Satisfactory, Conditional, or Unsatisfactory — based on a compliance review measured against the Appendix B factors across six regulatory areas (general/registration, driver, operational, vehicle, hazmat, and crash). A Conditional rating means deficiencies were found; an Unsatisfactory (or 'unfit') proposed rating leads to an order to cease operations if not corrected, and both are public and typically fail prequal outright. New entrants must pass a New Entrant Safety Audit within the first 12 months (Subpart D) covering essentials like the drug & alcohol program, DQ files, HOS records, vehicle maintenance, and insurance; automatic-failure items exist. Carriers can request an upgrade by submitting a corrective action plan (Safety Management Plan) with documented fixes. Because the rating and the CSA BASICs together decide the prequal grade, the whole documentation stack in these records is what an audit lives or dies on.
key_requirements: Pass the New Entrant Safety Audit within 12 months (Subpart D).
Maintain the six-area documentation the compliance review scores (Appendix B).
If Conditional/Unsatisfactory, submit a corrective action plan / Safety Management Plan to request upgrade.
forms: Corrective Action Plan / Safety Management Plan
deadlines: New Entrant audit within first 12 months
Upgrade requests per the notice timeline after a proposed rating
penalty_structure: An Unsatisfactory/unfit rating leads to an out-of-service order for the carrier; underlying violations carry their own civil penalties.
failure_points: New entrants failing the audit on automatic-failure items (no drug & alcohol program, no DQ files).
Leaving a Conditional rating unaddressed while prequal grades slip.
No corrective action plan documenting the fixes.
source: 49 CFR Part 385 incl. Appendices A/B; FMCSA
notes: Assembling the corrective-action documentation is core Origin work. Not legal representation. Reference only.

title: Part 172 Subparts H & I — Hazmat Training & Security Plan
applies_to: Any employer whose employees handle, offer, or transport hazardous materials in commerce (hazmat employees and hazmat employers).
summary: Subpart H (172.700-172.704) requires that every hazmat employee receive general awareness, function-specific, safety, security-awareness, and (if applicable) in-depth security training within 90 days of hire and at least every three years, with training records kept. Subpart I (172.800-172.804) requires certain shippers and carriers of higher-risk hazmat quantities to develop and adhere to a written SECURITY PLAN addressing personnel security, unauthorized-access, and en route security risks, and to train employees on it. Hazmat compliance is its own public CSA BASIC and a frequent prequal document request for carriers hauling placarded loads.
key_requirements: Train hazmat employees within 90 days of hire and recurrently (>= every 3 years).
Keep hazmat training records (172.704).
If handling covered quantities, develop and follow a written security plan (172.802).
Train employees on the security plan.
deadlines: Initial training within 90 days of hire; recurrent at least every 3 years
penalty_structure: Hazmat civil penalties are among the highest in the FMCSRs; scores in the Hazmat Compliance BASIC.
failure_points: No security plan where the quantity thresholds are met.
Expired or undocumented hazmat training.
source: 49 CFR Part 172 Subparts H & I; PHMSA/FMCSA
